title: [feature request] Swarm mode should support batch/cron jobs in addition to persistent services
body:
## Description

Today Swarm mode allows users to specify a group of homogenous containers which are meant to be kept running with the `docker service` CLI.  This abstraction, while powerful, may not be the right fit for containers which are _intended_ to eventually terminate or only run periodically.

Consider, for instance:
- An admin who wishes to allow users to submit long-running compiler jobs on a Swarm cluster
- A website which needs to process all user uploaded images into thumbnails of various sizes
- An operator who wishes to periodically run `docker rmi $(docker images --filter dangling=true -q)` on each machine
## Problem

Though some use cases could potentially be implemented by a service which pulls jobs off a distributed queue, there are some issues with this approach:
1. It adds an operational burden of creating, administrating, and ensuring the health of such a queue.  For many, this will kick up the barrier to entry of performing such tasks.
2. It does not necessarily ensure that failed jobs can be re-run the correct number of times or with the correct parameters.  Like above, this burden has now been offloaded to the user instead of being natively orchestrated.
3. It does not allow for easy customization of job parallelism settings.

Anything which is intended to be run periodically (such as the image garbage collection example above), could potentially cause a thundering herd problem if the scheduling is not handled by Swarm.  Imagine, for instance, that a user creates a `docker service` to periodically run a command inside the containers using normal old `cron`.  If these all wake up and attempt to execute at the same time during a time when production traffic is surging, it may be an issue for more critical production web services.  While it may help to mitigate the problem if the users do proper capacity planning and use flags such as `--reserve-cpu`, separating these concerns early on, especially when a temporal element is involved, seems to prudent.  (thanks to @jpetazzo who originally pointed out these concerns to me, and probably will have good insight as well)

This issue requests and outlines a proposed CLI, to get the ball rolling on discussion, track the issue, and gather information about potential use cases.
## Proposal

A new top-level command, `docker jobs`, could be introduced.  It would allow to specify that a container should be run X times, or every Y interval of time.  It could also be used to check up on these jobs.

Examples.

Run batch job once:

``` console
$ docker jobs create \
    -e S3_INPUT_BUCKET \
    -e S3_OUTPUT_BUCKET \
    -e IMAGE_NAME \
    nathanleclaire/convert
3x3bq2ibh1qe

$ docker jobs wait 3x3bq2ibh1qe; docker jobs ls
ID              NEXT PREV           FINISHED   FAILURES IMAGE
3x3bq2ibh1qe    -    3 seconds ago  1/1        0/1      nathanleclaire/convert 
```

Run batch job 16 times:

```
$ docker jobs create \
    --runs 16 \
    --parallel 3 \
    nathanleclaire/failer
bku4f1s1ncm0

$ docker jobs ls
ID            NEXT  PREV           FINISHED   FAILURES IMAGE
3x3bq2ibh1qe  -     2 minutes ago  1/1        0/1      nathanleclaire/convert 
bku4f1s1ncm0  Now   Now            4/16       6/10     nathanleclaire/failer
```

Run a task every hour:

```
$ docker jobs create \
    --every 1hr \
    nathanleclaire/hourlytask
ddh7pqvgbd8l

$ # One hour later...

$ docker jobs ls
ID            NEXT PREV         FINISHED  FAILURES IMAGE
3x3bq2ibh1qe  -    1 hour ago   1/1       0/1      nathanleclaire/convert 
bku4f1s1ncm0  -    1 hour ago   16/16     6/20     nathanleclaire/failer 
ddh7pqvgbd8l  1hr  1 minute ago 1/1       0/1      nathanleclaire/hourlytask
```

Interactively re-run a job:

``` console
$ docker jobs restart 3x3bq2ibh1qe
Running job 3x3bq2ibh1qe again from the beginning
```

Alternatively, `service` model could be expanded to accommodate this?  But it seems they would be easier to manage (for users) as separate things.

title: Dockerfiles and shell behavior
body:
There are currently two syntaxes for `CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT` (ignoring the interactions between the two instructions like passing options from `CMD` to `ENTRYPOINT`).
1. The exec format (JSON-style):

```
CMD ["executable", "flag" ]
```
1. The shell format

```
CMD /bin/true flag
```

Having both behaviors is confusing and unintuitive. We should settle on a single behavior preferably by having a lexer that recognizes and can parse appropriate shell commands and their flags from a variety of shells in either instruction.

As part of implementing this lexer we should deprecate existing behaviors carefully as this is a large breaking change. I'd suggest:
1. Major release with new syntax generates deprecation warning if old syntax is used.
2. Next major release removes old syntax and throws error message if used.

c.f. #1149 #2266

title: API PUT archive file ownership root when container running as non-root.
body:
We're having issues using the PUT /containers/(id)/archive endpoint due to file ownership permissions. When a container is running as a non-root user, the ownership is always reset back to root after uploading the file.

```
  > docker version                                                                         
Client:                                                                                    
 Version:      1.10.0                                                                      
 API version:  1.22                                                                        
 Go version:   go1.5.3                                                                     
 Git commit:   590d5108                                                                    
 Built:        Thu Feb  4 18:36:33 2016                                                    
 OS/Arch:      linux/amd64                                                                 

Server:                                                                                    
 Version:      1.10.0                                                                      
 API version:  1.22                                                                        
 Go version:   go1.5.3                                                                     
 Git commit:   590d5108-unsupported                                                        
 Built:        Fri Feb  5 02:32:52 2016                                                    
 OS/Arch:      linux/amd64  
```

Given an image with a directory owned by a different user

```
FROM ubuntu
RUN mkdir /opt/www-data && chown www-data:www-data /opt/www-data
docker build -t secure .
```

And a tar file owned by a non-root user

```
> touch test
> tar -zcvf test.tar.gz test

> ls -lha 
-rw-r--r-- 1 non-root non-root    0 Mar 30 10:19 test  
-rw-r--r-- 1 non-root non-root  114 Mar 30 10:19 test.tar.gz
```

When you launch the container as a non-root user

```
docker run -d -u www-data --name target secure sleep 100000
```

After uploading the tar, the file ownership permissions will be reset to root. The ownership should match either the original file or the user the container is being run as. 

```
curl -s -XPUT  -T test.tar.gz docker:2345/containers/target/archive?path=/opt/www-data
docker exec -it target bash

> /opt/www-data$ ls -lha
drwxr-xr-x 1 www-data www-data 4.0K Mar 30 10:24 .
drwxr-xr-x 1 root     root     4.0K Mar 30 10:22 ..
-rw-r--r-- 1 root     root        0 Mar 30 10:19 test 
```

title: Improve error reporting with --insecure-registry if https registry connection fails
body:
Follow up from #20253

Right now (docker 1.10.0) if docker can't connect to a registry using `--insecure-registry`, it gives the following error:

```
$ docker push loc2.loc/admin/repo
The push refers to a repository [loc2.loc/admin/repo]
Put http://loc2.loc/v1/repositories/admin/repo/: dial tcp 192.168.1.2:80: getsockopt: connection refused
```

This is very misleading because it looks like it's trying to connect to port 80 only and failing, but in reality there were two errors. The first error was that it failed to connect to port 443. This error message was lost. I expect to see both errors in this case so I know what docker is doing.

**Description**

Docker Swarm memory leak using Docker for AWS

Every iteration of "docker stack deploy --compose-file hello.yml hello" and "docker stack rm hello": all masters lose some memory (<100kb) and all nodes running the container lose around 1-2MB of memory. Eventually a node will run out-of-memory; and the out-of-memory node becomes unresponsive. Sometimes ASG terminates node immediately; sometimes it takes ASG time (over 1 hour) to auto-terminate the node. I've run this test on various Docker configurations: 1 master, 3 masters, 1 master and 1 worker, 3 masters and 3 workers.



**Steps to reproduce the issue:**
I have reproduced this out-of-memory in many docker configurations of master/worker combinations. I've used micro instances (500MB RAM) up to large instances (8GB RAM).  Running on master-only configuration with less instance memory runs into out-of-memory condition faster.
1. Create docker compose file - hello.yml:
```
version: '3.0'

services:
  hellotest:
    image: hello-world
    deploy:
      mode: global
      restart_policy:
        condition: on-failure
        max_attempts: 1
```
2. Create test shell script - test.sh
```
#!/bin/sh
##### globals #####
# how many times to loop through test
LOOPS=1000
 
starttime=`date`
echo start: $starttime
counter=1
while [ $counter -le $LOOPS ]
do
        echo loop number $counter
        # start docker
        cd /home/docker
        echo starting docker: docker stack deploy --compose-file test.yml hello${counter}
        docker stack deploy --compose-file test.yml hello${counter}
        sleep 5
        # stop docker
        echo stopping docker: docker stack rm hello${counter}
        docker stack rm hello${counter}
        sleep 5
        counter=$((counter+1))
done
 
endtime=`date`
```

3. Run shell script:
```
nohup ./test.sh &
```

Eventually a node will run out-of-memory.  I have stopped tests prior to out-of-memory condition.  Docker swarm does not release the memory.  I have pruned all docker resources - docker system prune. 
dockerd seems to be the process that consumes (and does not release) the memory

**Describe the results you expected:**

Docker swarm to release memory of unused resources.  I have not seen the memory loss in non-swarm configurations.

Happens every time.  I had a collegue run the same tests on a Centos server with a Docker swarm configuration.  Same issue.

title: Support --insecure-registry-ip=<CIDR>
body:
A sane reason to run insecure registries is when you trust your physical network.  In that case, your network is defined by CIDR ranges.

This whitelist would be applied post-DNS resolution.

As for port, all ports in the CIDR range would be trusted.  As the port is typically defined as part of the registry/image name, users are clear about who/what they are talking to.

This is forked from #8889.

title: named data volume instead of data container
body:
(This is a **feature request**)

Perhaps this was discussed somewhere, but I couldn't find something with a quick search.

I was under the impression that the new volume subsystem in 1.9 would replace the need for data-only containers. There are a couple of issues with the data-only containers approach. Basically the need is for a persistent named set of data volumes which are initialised with the contents of respective dirs in the base image. However data-only containers add noise to both the list of containers and the list of images, and prevent me from assigning meaningful names to data volumes.

Consider these two scenarios:
1. I need a persistent volume for storing uploaded images or I want to deploy my app code/jars somewhere but still be able to re-tweak the container using it.
2. I need a persistent volume for my mysql's `/var/lib/mysql`.

Unless I missed something, in the first case I can:
1. Create a named data volume.
2. Mount it when creating a container using the notation <volume name>:<path inside container>

In this case:
- `docker ps` will not show any redundant never-to-be-run containers.
- `docker volume ls` will be easy to interpret - I gave a name to this particular volume when I created it.
- `docker inspect` will easily show me that a container is using my named volume.
- `docker images` will remain clean and not retain unnamed images after retagging.

However now consider scenario no. 2, all that has really changed is that when I create this volume, I want it initialised from `/var/lib/mysql` of a particular image. However I am forced to do the following:
1. Create a "data only container".
2. Use the `--volumes-from` option when creating the app container.

In this case:
- `docker ps` shows x2 number of containers, and unless I choose a good naming scheme could end up very messy.
- `docker volume ls` shows a bunch of random ids that tell me nothing about what's inside those volumes or where I've mounted them.
- `docker inspect` again shows the random ids which are less helpful.
- `docker images` will show unnamed images, since if I make changes to the base image, I can't easily re-create the data-only container to use the new image with the existing volumes. This container sticks around pointing to the old image.

---

There are a couple of ways I can think of that can help here:
1. Simplest option IMO - provide a `volume rename` verb. This isn't the ideal solution, but I can easily script the rest. However even if using a different solution, I think this operation should be available regardless.
2. Add some option to initialise a new volume from a declared volume of some image. The problem here is that an image can declare several volumes and they have no names, so will have to be referred to by path. Not as convenient as the `--volumes-from` switch.
3. Add or tweak existing options to `run` or `create` to give names to certain volumes when they are auto-created and initialised just as they are now. This will replace the need for `--volumes-from` and data-only containers altogether. For example:
   
   ```
   docker run -d --name us.mysql -v us.data:/var/lib/mysql mysql 
   docker run -d --name eu.mysql -v eu.data:/var/lib/mysql mysql 
   ```
   
   Will result in the creation of two data volumes named `us.data` and `eu.data` _and_ their init from the contents of `/var/lib/mysql` of the `mysql` image _if_ they don't exist, or mount the existing ones if they already exist.
4. Another option I thought of is declaring "data volume sets" or "groups". Which basically completely replace data-only containers. In this case the commands might look something like:
   
   ```
   docker volume create-set --name us.mysql.data mysql
   docker run -d --name us.mysql --volumes-from us.mysql.data mysql
   ```
   
   In this case the `--volumes-from` refers to the set of data volumes which are collectively named rather than individually named. The only problem here is that it creates possible clashes between volume names and container names, perhaps a solution to that is a new `--volume-set` option instead.

title: update Google Cloud API client import paths and more
body:
The Google Cloud API client libraries for Go are making some breaking changes:
- The import paths are changing from `google.golang.org/cloud/...` to
  `cloud.google.com/go/...`. For example, if your code imports the BigQuery client
  it currently reads
  `import "google.golang.org/cloud/bigquery"`
  It should be changed to
  `import "cloud.google.com/go/bigquery"`
- Client options are also moving, from `google.golang.org/cloud` to
  `google.golang.org/api/option`. Two have also been renamed:
  - `WithBaseGRPC` is now `WithGRPCConn`
  - `WithBaseHTTP` is now `WithHTTPClient`
- The `cloud.WithContext` and `cloud.NewContext` methods are gone, as are the
  deprecated pubsub and container functions that required them. Use the `Client`
  methods of these packages instead.

You should make these changes before September 12, 2016, when the packages at
`google.golang.org/cloud` will go away.

title: Better Plugin Infrastructure
body:
As part of 1.11 we want to allow plugins lifecycle to be easily handled directly via the docker command line.

While using the docker cli, it should be made easy to do the following with plugins:
- discover
- download
- install
- enable/disable
- uninstall
- list installed plugins status

A new `plugin` verb may be added to the docker to cleanly separate the above.
## Impacts
- Unify the interface used to manage all thing docker related
- Make it easier to set a good practice of running plugin within containers
- Would allow auto-restart of crashed/stuck plugins
- One more verb to learn :)

title: DNS Flush / refresh - feature request
body:
We are seeing a variety of engagements where docker hosts participating in a swarm cluster somehow lose state in DNS,, thus containers on an overlay network fail to resolve other containers on the same overlay network.  The issue appears to be intermittent, but we have seen cases where all containers on a node have stopped resolving

Would like a less disruptive way to refresh/re-establish a functional DNS on a docker node than too restart the docker daemon, which is too disruptive for some customers.

This issue with varying similar circumstances is known to have occurred on many customer support engagements.  

Attempts to repro the issue within Docker labs thus far have not been successful, but here is a summary of the steps during a troubleshooting session that identifies the issue/symptoms

1) can deploy containers on existing and newly created overlays via compose, view networks, etc.  Nodes seems to be communicating fine with the controllers

2) Once multiple containers are deployed on existing overlay networks or on newly created overlays  via docker run or compose, during an unknown or specified timeline container(s) stop responding.  

3) confirm those failing containers by entering into a container that has been reported that is running,idocker exec -it <container_id> sh and running nslookup to the other container that exists on the overlay network

4) confirm container and overlays are being used by checking the output of docker inspect

Issue has been reported using engine 1.12.x

title: Can't use serial device in rootless docker with `dialout` group
body:
I have issues mounting a device with rootless docker through `--device /dev/ttyUSB0`. The device is accessible outside the docker to users of the `dialout` group. But I suspect the group is not properly propagated to the docker container. The device shows up as

```
crw-rw---- 1 nobody nogroup 188, 0 Nov 15 15:59 /dev/ttyUSB0
```

within the docker. On the host it is

```
crw-rw---- 1 root dialout 188, 0 Nov 15 07:59 /dev/ttyUSB0
```

Trying to access the device leads to a `Permission denied` error.

I am surprised the issue hasn't come up yet, as this seems to be a very common use case, but I couldn't find a similar issue yet.

I suspect it should be possible to pass the proper group mapping to the docker, but I couldn't figure out how to. I tried the `--add-group dialout` flag, but that only adds `root` (the user the docker is run as) to the `dialout` group, but won't affect the permissions of `/dev/ttyUSB0`.

**System information**

I run this on `Ubuntu 20.04.3 LTS`, docker version is `Docker version 20.10.10, build b485636` and the docker I run it on is based on `ros:noetic-ros-core`, should  be a pretty standard ubuntu 20.04 docker.

title: Cancelling pulls
body:
### Description

When I ask the engine to pull an image via `/images/create` with `fromImage`, it streams back update events. If I close the HTTP connection, the pull is cancelled. As far as I know, there is no other way to cancel a pull.

Suppose I'm making a UI application (like Docker Desktop, which I'm a maintainer of), and I want to be able to cancel pulls initiated through the UI. Currently, that's difficult - it's necessary to maintain a list of open HTTP requests, with mechanisms for searching and closing them, effectively duplicating data that already exists in the engine. It would be better if we could cancel pulls without needing a reference to any open HTTP connections. This becomes more valuable in combination with #45434.

### Proposal

- Add a new API endpoint (dubious strawman suggestion: `/images/create/cancel`). If I post to this, passing a string in the same format as the `fromImage` parameter of `/images/create`, any matching in-progress pulls should abort.
- When a pull is cancelled, any currently open HTTP connections from matching calls to `/images/create` should emit a cancellation event, and then the connection should close.

### Related issues

- #45434

title: Docker transparent bridge
body:
When I use Docker networking, I usually miss one feature I would call `transparent bridge`. I've been enlightened by [Virtualbox bridged networking](https://www.virtualbox.org/manual/ch06.html#network_bridged), so the basic idea is excerpted as follows,

_With potential `transparent bridge`, Docker would use a `networking plugin` on your host system that filters data from your physical network adapter._ 

_This allows Docker to intercept data from the physical network and inject data into it, effectively creating a new network interface in software. When a container is using such a new software interface, it looks to the host system as though the container were physically connected to the interface using a network cable: the host can send data to the container through that interface and receive data from it._ 

_This means that you can set up routing or bridging between the container and the rest of your network._

For this to work, Docker needs a `networking plugin`  on the host system. Is this kind of plugin already existing or beneficial to make?

title: Files with changed contents but identical metadata are not committed
body:
When committing a file with identical metadata in two subsequent layers, the second file's changes are discarded.
### System Configuration

Reproduced on both machines I tested on:
##### Machine 1:
- `docker 1.0.0`
- `--storage-driver=btrfs`
- `ubuntu 14:04`
- `Linux 3.13.0-30-generic #54-Ubuntu SMP Mon Jun 9 22:45:01 UTC 2014 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux`
##### Machine 2:
- `docker 1.2.0`
- `--storage-driver=btrfs`
- `ubuntu 14:04`
- `Linux 3.16.0-031600-generic #201408031935 SMP Sun Aug 3 23:36:11 UTC 2014 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux`
### To reproduce

1) Create files `A` and `B` containing different bytes, but having the following attributes in common:
- bytesize
- mtime (with second granularity; µsecs don't _seem_ to matter)
- mode
- owner/group

2) Write `A` into a container and commit to an image (`iA`).
3) Using the image `iA`, write `B` to the same path and commit the result as `iB`.
4) Run `iB` and print the file. Notice that the contents are the contents from the first layer.
### Minimal reproduction:

``` bash
#!/bin/bash
#
# This script creates two files with identical metadata in two subsequent layers.
# It prints the file as of the second layer, which actually prints the first file.
set -xeuo pipefail

workdir=/tmp/bug-workdir
mkdir "${workdir}"
trap "rm -rf ${workdir}" EXIT

cd "${workdir}"

mkdir p1 p2
cat > p1/go <<GO
#!/bin/bash
cp --archive /stage/file /file

cat > /file <<FILE
This file is from the first image. Its bytesize, mode, owner, and mtime are
identical to the file that should have replaced it in the second image.
....................................................................
FILE

touch -t 201409250000 /file
stat /file
GO

cat > p2/go <<GO
#!/bin/bash
rm -f /file
cp --archive /stage/file /file

cat > /file <<FILE
```

title: Better way to access the Engine API from a container
body:
Wouldn't it be nice if there existed an API access shim that one could use inside of a container without bind-mounting the socket and ensuring the client binary or libraries are compatible with the daemon you it happens to be talking to?

And, of course, it'd be critical to implement flexible access-control for what API calls are allowed.

One way to consider would be something as simple as:

``` shell
docker run --with-api-access-shim run <any_image> sh -c \
  "echo ps | socat - UNIX-CONNECT:/.docker.sock"
docker run --with-api-access-shim run <any_image> sh -c \
  "echo exec foo ls -la | socat - UNIX-CONNECT:/.docker.sock"
```

For those who need more, a shim shared library could be provided, with bindings for different languages.

title: FEATURE REQUEST: Support progress report when no TTY is available.
body:
Currently, Docker build suppresses progress output when running in a script, e.g. when triggered from Maven.
This is sane since otherwise the output would be garbled and weird.

However, it would be nice to have at least SOME output.

For example, I several times per day build a docker image with a build context of about 2 gigabytes. When building manually, I get a progress report for the "Sending build context..." part, but when running through Maven (which will automatically supply relevant --build-args) I get no output at all until the context is sent.

It would be nice to have at least something, like an output every 5% or so. 
The same goes for docker pull and any other progress report.

Thanks!

title: ANSI Code Page in Hyper-V Windows containers should not be 65001
body:
**Description**
When running a Windows container with Hyper-V isolation, the system ANSI Code Page (ACP) is set to 65001, which corresponds to the UTF-8 code page, rather than to an "ordinary" code page.

For Windows Desktop, this is a Beta feature called "Beta: Use Unicode UTF-8 for worldwide language support":

![Beta feature](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/139564/74662127-98957800-5199-11ea-9705-a119005bf9f8.png)

As this causes incompatibilities with software that doesn't support UTF-8, it should not be enabled in containers by default.
* Most notoriously, this happens with SQL Server: https://github.com/microsoft/mssql-docker/issues/466#issuecomment-506079975
* But it also affects other software: https://social.msdn.microsoft.com/Forums/en-US/0c4a2452-efd5-4e39-bd58-9748201e1670/codepages-in-servercorenanoserver?forum=windowscontainers
* Another example: https://github.com/conda/conda/issues/8088

**Repro steps without SQL Server:**
1. Execute `docker run -it --rm --isolation=hyperv mcr.microsoft.com/windows/servercore:1903 powershell`
2. Inside the PowerShell, run this:
```
$Signature = "[DllImport(`"kernel32.dll`")] public static extern int GetACP();";$acpGetter = Add-Type -MemberDefinition $Signature -Name "Acp" -Namespace Win32Functions -PassThru; $acpGetter::GetACP()
```
3. Observe the results

**Describe the results you received:**
* With process isolation: 1252 (an "ordinary" code page)
* With Hyper-V isolation: 65001 (the UTF-8 code page)

**Describe the results you expected:**
The selected code page shouldn't be determined by a beta feature that's not enabled on the host, regardless of the isolation mode. So it should either
* be the same as on the host OS (in my case, 1252),
* be hardcoded to something more friendly to non-UTF-8 applications,
* or be configurable at container start.

title: Cluster defaults should not be overridden by swarm init
body:
`swarm init` creates a `ClusterSpec` and overwrites the cluster's object spec with this one. This means defaults such as certificate validity period and task history retention are under the client's control. They should be under SwarmKit's control instead.

`swarm init` should only change values from the defaults when a value is given through a flag. Currently, it appears to overwrite the whole spec with the client-side defaults when no flags are specified.

cc @aluzzardi @tonistiigi

title: more docs for ulimit nproc
body:
The `nproc` setting for `--ulimit` seems to be a special case in that it is limited per user (and per process). As such if you start up multiple containers using the same uid, they are limited by the same `nproc` value, for example:

```
docker run -d -u daemon --ulimit nproc=3 busybox top
docker run -d -u daemon --ulimit nproc=3 busybox top
docker run -d -u daemon --ulimit nproc=3 busybox top
docker run -d -u daemon --ulimit nproc=3 busybox top
```

The last `docker run` will fail since each container is using the same uid, and nproc for that user has been limited to 3... this is, unfortunately, how the system handles `nproc`

Some extra docs explaining this would be extremely helpful.

Hello,

I try to configure the Docker daemon on **Debian 8.4** with **Docker 1.12.1**.

Note: I added a post on [Docker Community Forums](https://forums.docker.com/t/configure-docker-daemon-with-icc-and-disable-legacy-registry-on-debian-8-4/21073) but I got no answer.
# Goal

I would like to use the "icc" and "disable-legacy-registry" options of the Docker daemon. My aim is to be compliant with the rules of the Docker Bench for Security v1.1.0. In particular, I check the 2.1 and 2.13 rules.
# Issue

However, both options have no effect when using the "daemon.json" file or "docker.service" file.
# Tried solutions
## "docker.service" file
1. I replaced `ExecStart=/usr/bin/dockerd -H fd://` by `ExecStart=/usr/bin/dockerd -H fd:// --icc=false --disable-legacy-registry=true` in _/lib/systemd/system/docker.service_.
2. I execute `systemctl daemon-reload`
3. I execute `systemctl restart docker`

But when I execute "ps" I see that the launch command is correct: `/usr/bin/dockerd -H fd:// --icc=false --disable-legacy-registry`
## "daemon.json" file
1. I create _/etc/docker/daemon.json_ file and add: `{ "icc": false, "disable-legacy-registry": true }`
2. I execute `systemctl restart docker`

Rules 2.1 and 2.13 have still "WARN" status with Docker Bench for Security.

title: ZFS Storage Driver - ability to specify `parent dataset`?
body:
The [Docker ZFS storage driver docs](https://docs.docker.com/storage/storagedriver/zfs-driver/) specify how to use ZFS backed storage for Docker.

However, the implementation shown requires the ZFS pool to be dedicated to Docker.  There are many cases in which an administrator may want to use ZFS-backed storage for Docker but not want to allocate a separate pool.

As far as I can see, all the ZFS functions used by the storage driver will work at the `dataset` level (primarily `zfs clone`,  and `zfs snapshot`).

Would it be possible to amend the driver to support a `parent dataset` path?

For instance:

```json
{
  "storage-driver": "zfs",
  "storage-opts": [
       "size=200G"
       "zpool=data"
       "parent-dataset=docker"
    ]
}
```

The Docker storage would then be in  the `docker` dataset in the `data` pool.

title: Use UAC or create dedicated account during installation instead of asking for administrative account password
body:
When using volume mounts with Docker for Windows, the UI requires the user to enter their Windows username and password:

![Shared drives setting prompts for user's password](https://zmugkg.by3302.livefilestore.com/y3m26ckOwlhjlSV11vHJ9C3YoYHRbIaq67kXeoliwtiG_rCfVTUXq9qupdGmK9I7x9hL4x3fK7BkQ8CjNAri0aewwXI-80UyLvUflCH3gclFPI-vWnBlbYUYcN2gZ6oV5IcgyOhfMyD__qyyLDm1EWgm2nOQmwv0PruxO10pCOMeYc/Docker%20for%20Windows_2016-09-19_17-42-20.png?psid=1)

This seems like the wrong approach, since it results in problems for users that do not have passwords at all (i.e. use PINs or fingerprints), or have specific organizational requirements for their password that are incompatible with what the application can handle. There is a long thread where these issues are discussed [here](https://forums.docker.com/t/volume-mounts-in-windows-does-not-work/10693). See also #23992, where a number of people were having issues due to special chars in their passwords.

The experience would be better if the installer could create a "docker" user with the appropriate permissions during installation (since the installer runs in an elevated process) and use that for tasks like this later on. This way the user doesn't need to provide docker with an admin password (or even have one).

An alternative solution would be to perform tasks that require administrative privileges in elevated child processes. I'm unfamiliar with Go, but I know that when starting a process using the Windows ShellExecute API, setting the verb to "runas" will prompt the user for elevation and thereafter use an administrative user access token, allowing the new process to carry out volume mounting or user creation tasks.

The latter approach would mean the UAC prompt would appear every time administrative access is required, which is something I would personally prefer, but this might be seen as too inconvenient by others. It is possible for users to set their UAC notification level in Windows settings if they're in a sandbox environment and do not want to see every UAC prompt.

title: [Proposal] Handle "docker run --rm" inside the daemon instead of the client
body:
# The problem

Currently, docker handles the "--rm" on the client side, which means that the client will do the appropriate API calls to the daemon when it exits to remove the image on exit. This works great when you work locally in a simple setup, but may result in "garbage" containers existing forever under some circumstances. This may for example happen when:
- You connect through the TCP endpoints, either directly or through a tunnel, and loose the connection. (see #16546 for example)
- Your docker client crashes
- Your docker client gets killed for whatever reason
# The problem in our environment (CI)

Especially the last point hits me hard at the moment. We currently implement CI builds based on docker. The CI system calls a simple shell script, which builds the "builder" image and then runs it. The "builder" container is meant to be temporary and should vanish in case the build is finished or forcefully stopped (e.g. from the CI systems UI). We tried to use "run --rm" to accomplish this, which works fine when the build exits by itself. In case we externally stop the build, the CI system simply kills the script, which results in the "docker run --rm" process to die as well, but leaves the container running until it exits by itself. This leaves us with 2 problems: 
- The container is still running. This is already bad, but will get even worse in case one of our builds gets stuck, resulting in the container to run forever.
- The container won't be deleted on completion.

We also want to spawn temporary containers (e.g. databases for testing) on the host docker daemon from inside the "builder" container, which makes the problem even worse, as all these containers would live forever.
# Proposal/Feature request

When using "docker run", it should be possible to instruct the docker daemon what to do in case it looses the connection to the docker client. For example, we should be able to instruct the daemon to stop or kill and optionally rm the container on connection loss. This could for example look like:

```
docker run -ti --on-connection-loss=stop,rm myimage mycommand
```

I don't know much about the daemon internals or the API, so I can not really say how to implement it in a good way. One thing that I could imagine is an API call that says "do action X with name Y after Z seconds", where future calls to the same API with the same name Y would overwrite the old action and timeout Z. This would be comparable to TTL in services like etcd. The client could then do the following for the above "docker run" example:
- Create and start the container as usual
- After start, do an API call that says "stop and rm container after 30 seconds"
- Wait 15 seconds and do the API call again. Repeat forever, until exit.

"docker rm" supports the -v flag to also delete the container volumes. I would expect that the proposed feature would also support something like "rm -v".

body:
Preserving local files' UID/GID puts the docker user's UID into the container. title: Allow passing of container log timestamp to fluentd log driver
body:
Currently there is a limitation in fluentd where it does not support millisecond timing ( https://github.com/fluent/fluentd/issues/461 ). This causes some nonsense when using an ELK like backend when searching/reviewing logs. Docker emits the timestamp to the fluent-logger-golang, but this timestamp is converted to unix time ( seconds ) to work within the bounds of fluentd. Since docker already has the precise timestamp, it'd be great if this could be passed along as part of the log message data that gets emitted to fluentd so some post processing could be done after fluentd. 

I'm guessing it'd involve adding a new key in the map, https://github.com/docker/docker/blob/master/daemon/logger/fluentd/fluentd.go#L77 to include the msg.Timestamp. 

Thoughts?

title: BLOCKER: Docker forgets about volumes created with plugin drivers after service restart
body:
I created a plugin volume driver that stores volumes on a remote file system. I then created a standalone volume with the following command:

```
$ docker volume create --driver=my-driver --name=geo-vol --opt BindDirectory=/work/docker-dev/volumes/geo-vol
geo-vol
```

And it works:

```
$ docker volume inspect geo-vol
[
    {
        "Name": "geo-vol",
        "Driver": "my-driver",
        "Mountpoint": "/work/docker-dev/volumes/geo-vol"
    }
]
$ ls -al /work/docker-dev/volumes/geo-vol/
total 0
drwxrwxrwx 1 vagrant vagrant  68 Feb  3 19:19 .
drwxrwxrwx 1 vagrant vagrant 680 Feb  3 19:19 ..
```

I am able to mount the volume in multiple containers and read and write data from all the containers. It's a great way to share data between containers! But there's a problem...

```
$ docker volume inspect geo-vol
[
    {
        "Name": "geo-vol",
        "Driver": "my-driver",
        "Mountpoint": "/work/docker-dev/volumes/geo-vol"
    }
]
$ sudo service docker restart
docker stop/waiting
docker start/running, process 27923
$ docker volume inspect geo-vol
Error response from daemon: no such volume
$ docker volume ls | grep geo
[no output]
```

When restarting, Docker completely forgot that the `geo-vol` volume exists. But my driver didn't. When trying to re-create it:

```
$ docker volume create --driver=my-driver --name=geo-vol --opt BindDirectory=/work/docker-dev/volumes/geo-vol
Error response from daemon: The volume geo-vol already exists.
```

Looking through the HTTP logs for my driver, it's definitely working correctly. When it works (before Docker restarts), `docker volume inspect` calls my driver (as it should) to get the volume path:

```
Pid-28176 Thread-2 localhost-socket - - [04/Feb/2016 03:00:18] "POST /VolumeDriver.Path HTTP/1.1" 200 62 '{"Name":"geo-vol"}'
```

But when it doesn't work (after Docker restarts), `docker volume inspect` doesn't bother to call my driver. So the problem is definitely that Docker has forgotten the volume during restart, not that my driver is doing something wrong.

This is a major blocker for us. I'm going to have to revert our Docker environment to using data volume containers until this is fixed. :-(

**Description**

I'm creating this issue because we are having weird behavior with docker in swarm mode and I'm finally able to reproduce this so i thought I'd share my findings. I do realize this may have nothing to do with docker but please bear with me...

Run docker in swarm-mode, use say 6 nodes (3 managers, 3 workers) with an overlay network thats encrypted and attachable.

Run LOTS of one-off short-lived containers that attaches to the overlay network and does whatever task.

Wait a few hours and the overlay network begins to break down (some containers cannot reach each other, some containers misses dns records for services, running swarm services suddenly looses ability to talk to other services .. seems somewhat random)

Wait a few more minutes and syslog will be full of swarmnodes leaving and joining again and lots of "cannot allocate memory" messages from failed iptables commands, exec docker-init, exec docker-runc and so on...

This makes me think its an docker memory leak, but I'm not sure if its docker, the kernel or something else

**Steps to reproduce the issue:**
1. Buy 6 1gb memory, ubuntu 16.04.3 machines somewhere, swarm init and join them.
2. Create an overlay network `docker network create --driver overlay --attachable --subnet 10.51.192.0/20 --opt encrypted my-overlay`.
3. Run whatever helloworld test image just to have something to probe `docker service create --name web --network my-overlay --mode=global --publish 80:80 strm/helloworld-http`.

title: Proposal: Enhance Experimental Networking and Services UI
body:
- Add `--net=NETWORK`  where `NETWORK` is created via `docker network create`
- Update `--publish-service` to use `NETWORK:NAME` where `NETWORK` is the namespace under which to publish and `NAME` is the name of the service
### Example

```
docker network create mynetwork
# publish a service
docker run -itd --publish-service=mynetwork:web nginx
# publish a service (explicit network - it's optional but not required)
docker run -itd --net=mynetwork --publish-service=mynetwork:web
# consume a service only
docker run -itd --net=mynetwork busybox
```
### Failure Cases

```
# publishing a service on a network to which you don't belong
$ docker run -itd --net=not-mynetwork --publish-service=mynetwork:foo nginx
ERROR: You are not a member of the network "mynetwork"

# attempting to use null values in publish service to join a network, but don't publish a service
$ docker run -itd --publish-service=mynetwork: 
ERROR: You have not provided a service name. If you would like to join a network without publishing a service, please use the --net flag
```

These changes are motivated by https://github.com/docker/compose/pull/1676 and designed to accomplish the following [use cases](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1GO5AKQ22KohXWnKAUJjjgAecwlVqaHr9f44PLNpW51o/edit?usp=sharing)

We have deliberately ignored attachment to multiple networks at this time as there are concerns about how this is going to be implemented. 

Related to: https://github.com/docker/docker/pull/14143

Developed and discussed with @monadic @bboreham @squaremo @aanand @bfirsh @lxpollitt

title: [proposal] Expose layer IDs for images through the api
body:
The concept of layers was added in `v1.10` but there is currently no way to ask from the API what layers an image is using. This would make it possible to observe what layers are shared and validate that layers are the same as in registry/load tarball.

Ways to implement this:

2) Add `docker inspect --raw`. That would show the raw content addressable image config. This has an added benefit that you can verify that sha256 of this config makes up the image ID. Note that not all fields in `docker inspect` are in the raw config(there is no parent, tags etc.).

title: `docker rm thing` unmounts in the wrong order.
body:
The command `docker run -rm -v=/usr:/a -v=/etc:/a/lib base echo foo` has one mount inside another (you have to construct the directories carefully in order to avoid the bug mentioned in #3785).

The command runs, but fails when trying to destroy the container:

```
docker run -rm -v=/usr:/a -v=/etc:/a/lib base echo foo
foo
2014/01/27 16:25:01 Error: Cannot destroy container 08e0292e43c87013ff6e71f5d8b5ea90bf0dab84c97a2a3bfd58f8c8cbd93d94: Driver aufs failed to remove root filesystem 08e0292e43c87013ff6e71f5d8b5ea90bf0dab84c97a2a3bfd58f8c8cbd93d94: device or resource busy
```

(same result if you don't use the `-rm` argument, but do use `docker rm`)

I think what is happening is that docker is undoing the mounts in the wrong order. In general if `/a` and `/a/b` are both mount points, then `/a/b` should be unmounted before `/a`.

The diagnosis is complicated by the fact that the error message is unclear (like #3780)

(issue #3782 is somewhat related in that it involves mountpoints inside mounted filesystems on the container).

/cc @pwaller

title: Race condition, network interfaces
body:
Hello,
I've found a race condition that happens when I start a Docker instance. It seems Docker can set up network interfaces too late. It happened when I tried to launch a mumble server - murmur, using command
`docker run -t -i -p 64738:64738 a337fcd9ad07 murmurd`
Docker tried to execute it before setting up interfaces and of course, the server didn't listen on the expected port correctly. I have found a temporary workaround, using this command:
`docker run -t -i -p 64738:64738 a337fcd9ad07 /bin/bash -c "sleep 2;murmurd"`

title: Apply --volumes-from before creating volumes and don't error on overlap
body:
Use case: I'm Dockerizing the Prosody XMPP server which stores most of its configuration in files by default. Prosody comes with the prosodyctl administrative tool which creates/modifies files to affect administrative changes.

My Prosody image starts the server by default. It would be nice, though, if I could use the same image started with /bin/bash and --volumes-from <ID of production instance> to run administrative tools. Unfortunately, I get an error about overlapping volumes.

It would be nice if volumes configured in --volumes-from were applied first to an image on run. Then if the image tries to create a volume under the same mount point, creation of the new volume could be skipped. My assumption was that I could simply pull an old volume into a new container from the same image type without problems.

And yes, I know I can install the same packages into the new container. This is OK for simple setups, but anything more complex won't be as easy to work with. I could also create a second container for the purpose of running admin tools and using --volumes-from, but I'd rather just run the original container with /bin/bash and work with the data that way.

Thanks.

title: Registry URL's scheme should be the same as the Index
body:
The Registry URL's scheme is currently hardcoded to "https" whereas the Index' one is configurable (through the "DOCKER_INDEX_URL" env variable). Both scheme should be consistent at all time, it does not make sense to communicate with both entities with different level of security. Also it makes sense to be able to disable SSL if needed (for using the Registry on a private LAN for instance).

With the last version of the Registry, it's possible to emulate the Index routes from the Registry itself. In order to make it usable, being consistent on the scheme used becomes mandatory and the hardcoded one must be removed.

Earlier today, I ran into a problem accessing internal systems (example: redacted.lan) from inside containers on Ubuntu 16 and 14. (For detailed analysis, see: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/38902786/docker-container-cant-find-domain-on-private-network/38902944) I installed Ubuntu 14 from a fresh iso, and installed docker following the instructions from https://docs.docker.com/engine/installation/linux/ubuntulinux/. When my containers were running, they were not able to access (ping/nslookup/and so on) any internal systems due to not having the correct nameservers.

It turns out that Ubuntu uses a dnsmasq server running on `127.0.1.1` by default, which when docker starts up is filtered out. Then, having no nameservers, docker applies the defaults of 8.8.8.8 and 8.8.4.4, meaning that any internal services that would otherwise be findable are no longer so.

The "solution" I was able to figure out was to disable dnsmasq in `/etc/NetworkManager/NetworkManager.conf` however it seems more like a hack than a fix. I'm opening the issue to - at the very least - help others be aware of this situation.

title: Proposal: Image runtime dependencies
body:
## Image Runtime Dependencies

App deployments usually consist of multiple containers, a database, a caching server, app server, etc.
These are all runtime dependencies but the application defines these dependencies in a way that is only really visible to the developer (in their code)
### Proposal

Include a new `DEPENDS` command in the Dockerfile that would be used as such:

``` Dockerfile
FROM debian
# install my app

DEPENDS DB:3306 REDIS:6379 SOME_SERVICE
```

With this syntax, the image is declaring the containers it needs to have linked in in order to work.
We are declaring that we need something alaised as "DB" (from the link) which exposes port 3306. (docker run --link mysql:db)... likewise for redis (docker run --link redis:redis).
For "SOME_SERVICE" we are just saying we need this linked in, but we don't need care explicitly about what ports it exposes.

In all of these cases, if a link is not set, or the linked in item does not provide the requested port we would fail the "docker run"
This would also pave the way for a plugin or some other layer above Docker to do some sort of automatic dependency resolution

title: [epic] reduce redundant "fuzzy" lookups of containers (and other objects)
body:
### Description

For historic reasons, most objects have multiple identifiers;

- Name
- ID

Both of which must be unique, but when resolving objects, we allow fuzzy matching non-canonical identifiers to provide a more user-friendly UX; https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/c42005e94462596dfb00f82cfbe750f83e47948b/daemon/container.go#L30-L37


While this provides a friendly UX, the handling of non-canonical identifiers also made its way into many parts of the code. This has various consequences;

- Ambiguity; code does not always clearly advertise if a function only accepts an "ID", "Name", or also accepts non-canonical identifier (prefix / partial ID)
- (Partially because of the above) there's various code-paths where object resolution happens multiple times (function A resolves the ID, but passed it to a function that accepts "non-canonical" identifiers, therefore performing another lookup)
- Ambiguity has led to subtle bugs, where canonical identifiers were rejected because fuzzy matching resulted in ambiguous results (see for example [#48669](https://github.com/moby/moby/pull/48669), [#48670](https://github.com/moby/moby/pull/48670)

We should improve this situation and, where possible, use canonical IDs, but in places where non-canonical IDs are needed make sure that it's clearly advertised as such. In future, we may consider having an explicit type for identifiers to provide flexibility, but maintaining a user-friendly UX (such as reporting a human-readable name instead of ID where suitable, but preserving the ID for logic handling the identifier).

Here's a (non-exhaustive) list of things we could look into:

- [ ] reduce ambiguity: rename arguments that accept "fuzzy" identifiers
    - use "id" (and similar, like `containerID`) only for places where only an ID is accepted
    - explicitly use (e.g.) `prefixOrName` for places where the argument accepts a non-canonical ("fuzzy") identifier
    - clearly document _intent_: in places where non-canonical / fuzzy identifiers are _required_ (by design), make sure that the function description clearly outlines _why_ it's needed.
- [ ] reduce repeated lookups
    - where possible, resolve IDs early; validate early, fail fast, so that the user gets informed when providing invalid identifiers (e.g. on "create", not "start" for containers).
    - internal methods and functions should use a canonical identifier where possible
    - :point_up: care should be taken when _storing_ identifiers: some user-provided identifiers are "dynamic" by design, and should be resolved when used (to allow, e.g. objects to be replaced (network aliases etc.))
    - :point_up: :point_right: but we may need to revisit some designs and make sure they're matching the original intent: for example, should `--network=container:<some container>` and `--volumes-from=<some container>` be "dynamic" or "immutable"?
- [ ] validate IDs in functions that only accept canonical IDs
    - functions accepting an ID should never accept a non-canonical ID. e.g., a function accepting an ID should reject an ID-prefix (short ID); it's the caller's responsibility to resolve the ID before calling.
- [ ] consider introducing a "object-identifier" struct to combine "name" and "id"
    - while "ID" can be considered the most canonical for most places, it's not the most user-friendly presentation
    - having a type that provides both the unique ID _and_ a (user-facing) name can help with this (e.g. `struct{ID string, Name string})
    - :point_up: the `ID` stored MUST always be in its canonical form (i.e., no "prefix")
    - :point_up: similarly, the `Name`, when resolved, MUST be stored in its canonical form (no "prefix" or "partial" matches)
    - :question: Should this type be "declarative" (for better words)? For place where we want to present / differentiate between "user-provided" information and "resolved" information, do we need to store _both_? This would also allow detecting if an ID is canonical, or "to be resolved", and may also allow for "re-resolving".

Hello there,

I am running my test "microsoft/iis" container with following command with "--cpus 16" limitation:
```
docker run -d  --name gt_test_iis --cpus 16 microsoft/iis ping -t localhost
```

Looks like "--cpus" works fine and when I run my `simulate_cpu_load.ps1` script:
```
ForEach ($Number in 1..16){

   }
}
```

```
unknown flag: --cpus
See 'docker update --help'.
```

Thoughts?

title: Network "Created" time can change, and even go backwards!
body:
**Description**

After creating a swarm network, I would expect the `Created` time to be fixed. In fact, it goes backwards and forwards.

**Steps to reproduce the issue:**

On a single-node swarm:

```
$ docker network create -d overlay testnet
ggx5vityxoi9i2u5efehmqmdy

$ docker network inspect testnet --format '{{.Created}}'
2018-07-17 13:40:22.066855102 +0000 UTC

$ docker service create --name test --network testnet alpine top
nhwivrl9qxc0159wp72eh7acc

$ docker network inspect testnet --format '{{.Created}}'
2018-07-17 13:41:12.487659795 +0000 UTC
```

Note that the network creation time was `13:40` and is now `13:41`.

We can also make time go backwards:

```
$ docker service update test --replicas=0
test

$ docker network inspect testnet --format '{{.Created}}'
2018-07-17 13:40:22.066855102 +0000 UTC
```

Now it's `13:40` again!

**Describe the results you received:**

The network's creation time keeps changing.

**Describe the results you expected:**

I assume it should be the time I created the network with `docker network create`.

**Additional information you deem important (e.g. issue happens only occasionally):**

I guess this is because there are really two network objects: the network in the SwarmKit raft store (with the original time) and the engine network that exists on nodes which have containers connected to the network. Perhaps `docker network inspect` prefers to show the engine network when available, or the SwarmKit one if not?

To avoid confusion, perhaps the engine network should be created with the same time-stamp as the swarm one?

This might also explain why the `Labels` field changes between `null` and `{}`.

title: Avoiding private registry hostname in FROM directive of Dockerfile
body:
Say I have an image FOOBASE in a private registry (hostname:port PRIVREGHOSTNAME:5000)

I want to use this image in a Dockerfile for a new image FOONEW. Currently, it is done as follows:
# Dockerfile

FROM PRIVREGHOSTNAME:5000/FOOBASE
...

That is, the hostname of the private registry is in the Dockerfile.

Now say, I want to change the registries. I have to change the Dockerfile of FOOBASE, rebuild it, and rebuild the image FOONEW that depends on FOOBASE. Obviously, changing the Dockerfile is not desirable. The registry hostname should not be in the Dockerfile

Instead, a better solution is to define a new parameter --registry-url for docker build. E.g.,

docker build -t . --registry-url PRIVREGHOSTNAME:5000

So by default, the image referenced in Dockerfile is searched first in the registry-url and then in Dockerhub.

title: Link containers with --net=host
body:
I was wondering why linking a container using the bridge networking to a container using the host networking doesn't work.

The use case is simple: I have a first container running a service on a port and a second container accessing this service and internet. The work done by the second container is limited by the speed of the network, so I would like to switch to host networking to see if it makes a difference.

I reproduced my tests using phusion/baseimage. In these examples, the service provided by the first container will be ssh.

I would like to know if you had similar issues and how you approached the problem.
## Initial configuration

This is the configuration with the bridge networking. As expected, the second container receive the right environment variables.

First container

``` bash
#!/bin/bash -ex

sudo docker stop test_a || true
sudo docker rm test_a || true
sudo docker run  -t --name test_a --publish=22 phusion/baseimage:0.9.10
```

Second container

``` bash
#!/bin/bash -ex
```

If I don't publish the port on the first container, the link works (the second container receives the environment variable `TEST_NAME=/test_f/test`) but as expected the second container doesn't receive the ip of the first one.

First container

The documentation says that "_Publishing ports and linking to other containers will not work when sharing the host's network stack._" but also that "_With the networking mode set to host a container will share the host's network stack and all interfaces from the host will be available to the container._"

If _all_ the interfaces are available, it also means that the second container will have access to the `docker0` interface and have access to the first container using the bridge networking. title: Containers take take a very long time to stop after all processes in them have exited
body:
This may be related to #34097, as the symptoms are very similar to those reported. However, I was instructed to open a new ticket. 

Summary:

- Run `docker stop -t 6`
- Logs confirm that SIGTERM is sent to the container
- The `top` command shows that all processes in the container exit almost immediately after they receive the SIGTERM.
- The `docker ps` command shows the container is still running long after all processes have exited. 
- From the daemon logs, an attempt is made to force the container down after the 6 second timeout expires. 
- The container takes as much as 1.5 minutes to stop, after the daemon tries to force it down. 
- Changing the timeout (e.g. 20 sec) makes not difference. 
- Using `docker kill -s TERM` followed by `docker kill` (after timeout) behaves the same as `docker stop -t <timeout>`. 

The main process in the container spawns all the other processes, and waits for a terminate or interrupt signal. When it's received, it terminates all child processes and exits. Running the `top` command on the host, and filtering the output for the `uid` used in the container, shows all container processes quickly exiting after the `stop` command is run. The container logs also confirm that the shutdown process occurred as expected. 

There are between 2-15 containers running in a group. When only 3 or 4 containers are run, they shutdown as expected. CPU and memory usage are high with all 15 instances running, but not higher than expected and well below the maximum supported by hardware. 

I restarted the daemon in debug mode. After 6 seconds the logs show:

> failed to exit within 6 seconds - using the force

The same message occurs for each container in the group. 

Immediately after it prints for a single container:

> kill failed because 'container not found' or 'no such process'

About a 1:20 minutes later:

> Container <id> is not running

This message was for a different container ID than the previous one. 

No other warning or error messages.

This behavior is very consistent, and sometimes results in other non-docker terminal commands taking a very long time to execute while it's occurring. 

**Platform:** 

- CentOS 7.5, on a single bare-metal server (no swarm)
- Server version: 18.03.1-ce
- Kernel version: 3.10.0-862.3.3.el7.x86_64
- Storage driver: overlay
- Backing filesystem: xfs

I tried this on a system running `17.04` as well, with the same results. 

**Note:** This is an air-gap system, so I'm not able to copy and paste logs or command output. 

A couple question I have are:

- What exactly does Docker do when stopping a container?
- What constitutes the container being "stopped"?

title: Feature Request: export more of the docker compose loader functions
body:
Can we export more of the docker/cli/compose/loader functions, to allow partial element decoding.

Reasoning:

we may not like the compose format that much, but it is an industry standard.  Now there are various docker provided libraries for unmarshalling the format, but the new compose library in the docker cli should likely become a standard.

Currently the only exported method is really the `Load()` method, which unmarshalls an entire compose file.  This is done because in legacy files, there was so much interconnection between the services, and the networks, that it was impossible to consider a single service or network on it's own.  Those reasons are no longer a problem now that the v3 files do away with the keys that required such interconnection (links, volumes_from.)
Or can we separate that loading code to it's own library (which would allow easy future deprecation anyway.)

Can we export any of the following functions, to give other software core decoding functionality?  

```
loadServices()
loadService()
loadNetworks()
loadVolumes()
loadSecrets()
```

If these methods were exported, then other projects could integrate the industry format into their own yml configurations, using the core code and not having to rewrite that code, or hack their formats to match the requirements for the Load() method.

The value gained would be easy reuse of the compose loader, to provide structs that can then be used to directly run client operations by mimicking the CLI.

title: [docs] "Best Practices" should mention SHELL instruction
body:
https://docs.docker.com/develop/develop-images/dockerfile_best-practices/#using-pipes

I think this should mention 

    SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-c"]

as an alternative to make `set -o pipefail` work on Debian base images. Using the exec form, especially when you have the need to add pipefail to an existing long RUN sequence, is intrusive and would incur a lot of rewriting work.

title: Initialize volumes when mounted to a host directory
body:
According to the [documentation](https://docs.docker.com/userguide/dockervolumes/#data-volumes), new volumes should be initialized with the contents of the base image in the volume location.

This indeed works when running `docker -v /path/inside/container ...`, but not when running `docker -v /path/on/host:/path/inside/container ...`.

The documentation doesn't mention there should be a different behavior, so we should either:
1. Update the documentation to mention that the behavior is different when the volume is bound to a host directory
2. Find a way to initialize the volume when binding it to a host directory. Perhaps if the host directory does not initially exist, or with an extra `docker` flag?

body:
I compared network bandwidth between two hosts(named A ran netperf and B ran netserver) to bandwidth between container(started with docker on host A, run netperf) and host B(run netserver).
A and B used a direct 10Gbps Ethernet link between two 82599es NICs.
The netperf command at client is "netperf -H serverip -t TCP_STREAM -l 120 -- -m 4096", and command at server is "netserver".
The network bandwidth between two hosts is 9.61Gbps , the result between container and host is 6.37Gbps lower than 30% of the host.

I found enable RPS and RFS for veth can improve transmit network throughput, but also reduced receive network throughput. RPS and RFS can not benefit transmit or receive at the same time. The follow table shows my test result.

The purpose of RPS and RFS is distribute the work across multiple processors, so i think CPU is not the major factor result in container's performance degradation.
Is there any other way to improve performance?

title: Docker Swarm service restarting on stack deploy without changes
body:
### Description

`docker stack deploy` followed by `docker service update` change order of mounted volumes causing subsequent `docker stack deploy` doing a restart of a service.

### Reproduce

Create the following `docker-compose.yaml`:
```
services:
  test:
    image: alpine
    command: tail -f /dev/null
    volumes:
      - ./2:/2
      - ./1:/1
      - ./3:/3
```
Execute the following script:
```bash
#!/bin/bash

for i in {1..3}; do
  mkdir -p "$i"
done

docker stack deploy -c docker-compose.yaml --prune my-stack --detach=false
docker service inspect my-stack_test --pretty > first.spec
echo "first stack deploy done"
sleep 10
docker service update --force my-stack_test
docker service inspect my-stack_test --pretty > second.spec
diff first.spec second.spec > first_to_second.diff
echo "force update done - expected restart happened"
sleep 10
docker stack deploy -c docker-compose.yaml --prune my-stack --detach=false
echo "second stack deploy done - unexpected restart happened"
docker service inspect my-stack_test --pretty > third.spec
diff second.spec third.spec > second_to_third.diff
diff first.spec third.spec > first_to_third.diff
```

Check output of `docker service ps my-stack_test` and find that it shows two shutdown and one running service instance where it should only show two.

### Expected behavior

`docker stack deploy` without changed service definition should never restart services.
More clearer: `docker service update` and `docker stack deploy` should create the same order of volumes in the spec.

Since we upgraded to Docker 1.7.0 (from 1.6), docker-compose to 1.3.1 (from 1.2), and started killing containers instead of stopping them (faster, remove them anyway), we twice had containers failing to start with the following message from compose:

title: Docs: improve documentation for developing volume plugins
body:
Hi fellow volume plugin developers!

I'm currenty writing my first volume plugin and I have some questions that are not really answered in the API documentation. I will send a pull request that clarifies these points because I think it will also help others:

On .Create I create a special device, let's call it /dev/specialdev_name and put a file system on top of it.
On .Mount I mount it and reference count for the name. The first .Mount really mounts the file system, further .Mounts increase the refcount.
On .Umount I decrease the refcount and if 0, I umount the /dev/specialdev_name
On .Remove I remove the /dev/specialdev_name if the refcount is 0/is not mounted, otherwise I set Err.

So far so easy, the problem are .Path (and .Get and .List). To me it is not clear how to react if a volume is known to the driver (i.e., it was created with .Create), but is currently _not_ mounted. Should I report the "Mountpoint" where it will be available after a .Mount, or set "Err"? The same question applies for .Get. For .List it seams that I should include volumes known but not mounted, otherwise they don't show up in "docker volume ls". But yeah, it all boils down to this "known to the plugin and created, but currently not mounted" situation. Set Mountpoint to where it will be available after .Mount? Or set Mountpoint to ""? Or even set Err?

title: Allow bind mounting to container's root (/)
body:
I would like to request a new feature. Currently, if I try to mount (type bind) a directory to a root (`/`) of a container, I get an error that I cannot do that. But I find this a very useful approach to move legacy virtual machines and OpenVZ containers to Docker. I can just copy their contents to a directory on a host and then mount it into an [empty Docker image](https://hub.docker.com/r/tozd/empty/). I use `/sbin/init` as a command and the old legacy system starts.

I know that this work well because currently I mounted each top-level directory separately. But this is error prone and unnecessary. It would be great if I could mount one directory to a root.

I understand that this diminishes a lot of things Docker ecosystem provides, but it is a great way to transition slowly legacy systems into Docker infrastructure.

```
BINDDIR := $(if $(DOCKER_HOST),,bundles)
```

to

```
BINDDIR := bundles
```

title: Fast update service in loop broke swarm
body:
I used the following simple loop to make a few quick changes to an environment:

```
REG_URL=[docker_image_url]

for service in `docker service ls|grep '/image_name:'|awk {'print $1'}`
do
  docker service update $service --image $REG_URL
  docker service update $service --env-add LOG_ENTRIES_KEY=ABCD1234
done
```

After running this script, I was no longer able to communicate from the manager node to any swarm node, getting a timeout error for simple commands like `docker service rm`

The same script without adding another environment variable works fine and causes no issues.

I suspect that running the update service with two flags on one command would have worked fine; although I didn't try, running it as two commands should not cause nodes to become unavailable.

Perhaps something is causing a problem if the first update command hasn't completed on the backend while the second one attempts to run?

I was only able to recover the swarm by running `docker swarm leave` on each node, and readding them..

title: Include More Information in Daemon Logs
body:
Recently at work was prompted at work to tail the docker daemon logs to investigate an condition (which was sorted out) I had the daemon running on `debug` mode and I found some information missing that could have been useful in debugging, to explain what I mean let me elaborate: 

Our Docker use case can be termed as command and control where we have a set of master instances talking to a bunch of minions who instruct the minions to perform image/container management (pull, push, start, kill) to aid, debug and potentially leave a log-trail of command origin it will be very useful to list the source of the command to the docker daemon for example current daemon logs look like:

![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/311217/4878297/474f709e-6307-11e4-8604-ddd648c1bc29.png)

These log fragments provide what command was executed but does not provide clue about its origin as in whether it came from localhost or remote host. I also saw that the future releases will contain a enhanced and a more parsable log format #8761 which is awesome but I feel that providing the source where the command came from will be useful as well in establishing an log-trail about container management.

```
# syntax = docker/dockerfile:1.0-experimental

RUN cat /secret/test.secret && ls -l /secret
```

```
echo "THIS IS A SECRET" > secret.file
```

```
DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 docker build --no-cache -t secret-test --progress=plain --secret id=test.secret,src=secret.file .
```

title: NVIDIA GPU support
body:
Hello, author of [nvidia-docker](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-docker) here.

As many of you may know, we recently released our NVIDIA Docker project  in our effort to enable GPUs in containerized applications (mostly Deep Learning). This project is currently comprised of two parts:
- A Docker volume plugin to mount NVIDIA driver files inside containers at runtime.
- A small wrapper around Docker to ease the deployment of our images.

More information on this [here](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-docker/wiki/Internals)

While it has been working great so far, now that Docker 1.12 is coming out with configurable runtime and complete OCI support, we would like to move away from this approach (which is admittedly hacky) and work on something which is better integrated with Docker.

The way I see it would be to provide a prestart OCI hook which would effectively trigger our implementation and configure the cgroups/namespaces correctly.

However, there are several things we need to solve first, specifically:
1. How to detect if a given image needs GPU support
   Currently, we are using a special label `com.nvidia.volumes.needed`, but it is not exported as an OCI annotation (see https://github.com/docker/docker/issues/21324)
2. How to pass down to the hook which GPU should be isolated
   Currently, we are using an environment variable `NV_GPU`
3. How to check whether the image is compatible with the current driver or not.
   Currently, we are using a special label `XXX_VERSION`

All of the above could be solved using environment variables but I'm not particularly fond of this idea (e.g. `docker run -e NVIDIA_GPU=0,1 nvidia/cuda`)

So is there a way to pass runtime/hook parameters from the docker command line and if not would it be worth it? (e.g. `--runtime-opt`)

title: Auth plugin receives empty request body if transfer-encoding=chunked
body:
**Description**
Docker (the service) accepts requests with "Transfer-encoding: chunked". However the authorization plugin doesn't: 
https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/master/pkg/authorization/authz.go#L58
It expects Content-Length to be set. If that header is not set (i.e. when transfer-encoding: chunked), it wrongly assumes a nil body. 

This leads to issues with libraries such as docker-java and projects building on top of it such as testcontainers-java. Both supported clients in docker-java (okhttp and apache-http) are sending content with transfer-encoding: chunked. 

**Steps to reproduce the issue:**
1. Setup an authorization plugin, e.g. https://github.com/ad-freiburg/docker-no-trivial-root 
2. Issue a create call with transfer-encoding: chunked (here with curl, simulating the docker-java code)
```
curl -v -H 'Content-type: application/json' -H 'Transfer-encoding: chunked' localhost:2375/containers/create -d '{"Image": "ubuntu:latest"}'
{"message":"plugin no-trivial-root failed with error: AuthZPlugin.AuthZReq: unexpected end of JSON input"}
```
AuthZ Request debug dump: 
``` (authorization.Request) {
  User: (string) "",
  UserAuthNMethod: (string) "",
```

The plugin failed to parse the request as it receives a nil request body (while it is not)

title: docker container is privileged tries to assume more capabilities than available
body:
tl;dr is that `docker run --privileged` tries to assign all known caps, while `dockerd` itself might not have all caps already.

Background: [Talos](https://www.talos.dev/) in new version 0.13 started dropping two capabilities (kexec + module loading) from all processes but PID 1. Talos itself doesn't use `dockerd`, but if I launch privileged pod on Kubernetes with `docker:20.10-dind` image, I can't run any privileged container inside:

```
/ # docker run -it --rm --privileged alpine
docker: Error response from daemon: OCI runtime create failed: container_linux.go:380: starting container process caused: apply caps: operation not permitted: unknown.
```

The problem starts in https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/306fa44b7ca59282dc8695e6d169c5b25698d0cb/daemon/exec_linux.go#L25

Which essentially uses the list of capabilities built here:
https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/306fa44b7ca59282dc8695e6d169c5b25698d0cb/oci/caps/utils.go#L23-L37

This list contains every capability present on the host, which might be not be true (as some capabilities might have already been dropped).

Containerd OCI does proper thing:

https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/d193dc2b8afb1467255cea5326e9807514f94c0f/pkg/cap/cap_linux.go#L123-L136

I'm happy to send a PR, but what is the best way to solve this in the docker codebase?

title: Many parallel calls to `docker exec` make Docker unresponsive
body:
### Description

Since today, we've experienced a problem where our CI system could no longer run our tests properly.

After a bit of investigation, we found how to resolve it, but not the root cause. This happens on two independent servers, one on Ubuntu 22.04, the other on 18.04. Both are running Docker 24.0.1.

Essentially, we're launching an image of SQL Server using a tmpfs volume for the data files. Before the tests, we're creating a database with seed data. Then, for every test run, we run `docker exec` to copy the data (and log) files, and attach them as a new database. This is running in parallel without any concurrency limit, and has worked before.

Now we found that when doing this, all Docker commands become unresponsive after a short time. E.g. `docker stats` no longer refreshes correctly and shows only dashes `--` instead of the actual information:
![image](https://github.com/moby/moby/assets/10274404/30c04cc6-188f-4182-a8ab-249d6ad9633c)

Other Docker commands, e.g. `docker stop` take extremely long (if they finish at all). The tests run usually in 10 minutes, now it takes several hours with most tests failing due to a timeout exception when calling Docker commands from within the test suite. 

### Reproduce

1. First I'm starting SQL Server
```bash
docker run -e ACCEPT_EULA=Y -e "SA_PASSWORD=yourStrong(#)Password" \
--mount type=tmpfs,destination=/var/opt/mssql/data \
--mount type=tmpfs,destination=/var/opt/mssql/log \
--mount type=tmpfs,destination=/var/opt/mssql/secrets \
dangl/mssql-tmpfs:latest
```
2. Then I'm creating a quick script to just do some `cp` operations via `docker exec` in parallel:
```bash
touch concurrent_exec.sh
for i in {1..50}
do
  echo "docker exec <CONTAINER_ID> sh -c \"cp /var/opt/mssql/data/master.mdf /var/opt/mssql/data/$i.mdf\" &" >> concurrent_exec.sh
done
echo "docker exec <CONTAINER_ID> sh -c \"cp /var/opt/mssql/data/master.mdf /var/opt/mssql/data/last.mdf\"" >> concurrent_exec.sh
```
3. Now I execute `sh concurrent_exec.sh` and watch the output of `docker stats` in another session. `docker stats` will freeze for a time (but eventually recover). It takes longer the more parallel operations I do.


The actual behavior depends on how many parallel calls I'm making. E.g. with `5`, there's no (noticeable) interruption, with `50` it already blocks for around a minute.

_No response_

title: Swarm mode: Election delay on startup with single manager
body:
Using **docker master**.

**Steps to reproduce the issue:**
1. Start a single node Manager.
2. Restart it.

**Describe the results you received:**

It will wait for the whole `ElectionTick` delay to reelect itself and accept new requests. This is due to the node going down and assuming it is part of a multi-node cluster waiting for a message from a possible new leader.

**Describe the results you expected:**

The node restarts and elects itself instantly as it is the only member in the raft memberlist.

**Solution:**

Artificially advance the state machine for the number of steps to trigger an Election when we restart and the Manager is the only member of the raft.

/cc @icecrime @aaronlehmann
